A ball strikes a horizontal surface with momentum p at an angle θ to the surface, as shown.

The ball rebounds with the same magnitude of momentum at an angle θ to the surface.
The ball is in contact with the surface for time t.
What is the magnitude of the average resultant force acting on the ball during the collision?

hints: Notice $\theta$ is measured to the surface, not to the normal, so resolve each momentum $p$ into a parallel part $p\cos\theta$ and a perpendicular part $p\sin\theta$.
Compare before and after along each direction: the component parallel to the surface stays the same, while the component perpendicular to the surface reverses in direction.
Use impulse as change in momentum, $F = \Delta p/t$, applied to the perpendicular direction where the change is the final value minus the initial value.
walkthrough: Take upwards perpendicular to the surface as positive. Each momentum $p$ at angle $\theta$ to the surface has perpendicular component $p\sin\theta$ and parallel component $p\cos\theta$.

Before impact the perpendicular momentum is $-p\sin\theta$ (downwards) and after rebound it is $+p\sin\theta$ (upwards). The parallel component $p\cos\theta$ is in the same direction before and after.
The change in momentum is $\Delta p =$ final momentum $-$ initial momentum. Parallel change is zero. Perpendicular change is $\Delta p = (+p\sin\theta) - (-p\sin\theta) = 2p\sin\theta$.
Average resultant force magnitude is rate of change of momentum: $F = \Delta p/t = 2p\sin\theta/t$, directed normal to the surface with units $\text{N}$.

A.explanation: Momentum is a vector. The direction changes on rebound, so the change in momentum and the resultant force are not zero.

B.explanation: This ignores the angle $\theta$ to the surface and treats the whole momentum $p$ as reversed, which only applies for normal incidence.

C.explanation: The term $p\cos\theta$ is the component parallel to the surface, which is unchanged in the rebound and so contributes no change in momentum.

D.explanation: The perpendicular component $p\sin\theta$ reverses from downwards to upwards, giving change $2p\sin\theta$ and force $2p\sin\theta/t$.
